planting.note: Seed has a hard coat and benefits from mechanical scarification plus a winter outdoors before spring germination; mimics natural freeze-thaw cycling on exposed scree.

directions: Scarify seed lightly with sandpaper before sowing into gritty, fast-draining mineral soil, as this ground-hugging milkvetch rots quickly in rich or wet substrates. Site on an exposed, sun-baked slope or gravel bar that mimics the limestone and shale outcrops of its Black Hills home range. Established clumps need almost no supplemental water once rooted and resent any summer irrigation. Expect a slow-building cushion of silvery pinnate foliage topped by magenta-purple racemes in its second or third season.
sources: Center for Plant Conservation plant profile

planting.note: Mustard-family seed needs a cold, moist winter stratification period outdoors before it will germinate reliably the following spring.

directions: Press seed onto lean, rocky or shaly mineral soil in fall and let winter weather do the stratification work on this low rosette-forming crucifer. It thrives on exposed limestone and igneous outcrop ledges with sharp drainage and minimal organic matter. Bright yellow four-petaled flowers appear close to the ground in early spring, followed by the characteristic double-chambered inflated seedpods that give the species its name. Keep it dry and uncrowded by taller vegetation; it does not compete well in fertile garden beds.

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall so seed receives natural winter chilling; spring sowing without a cold treatment gives poor, erratic germination.

directions: Give this silvery-leaved mustard full sun and coarse, gravelly soil that drains instantly after rain, as it is adapted to thin granitic and shale substrates on open slopes. Established plants form a dense mat of felted rosettes and need no watering beyond natural rainfall once past their first season. Clear yellow flowers open in early spring and are followed by the inflated, double-lobed seedpods that make the plant easy to identify and collect seed from. It is an excellent, tough choice for a sunny scree bed or dry rock garden pocket.

planting.note: Fall sowing onto bare, open mineral soil lets seed overwinter naturally; this species self-sows readily once established on disturbed, dry ground.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil on an open, sun-baked slope, since this bristly borage native to dry buttes and grassland edges resents shade and rich, moisture-retentive beds. Its whitish, tightly clustered flower spikes resemble a candle or cockscomb and are most striking against bare gravel or rock. Water only to establish the first season; thereafter it tolerates extended drought typical of the Black Hills foothills and surrounding plains. It behaves as a short-lived perennial or biennial, so allow some seed to drop each year to maintain a stand.
